# Kasibhāradvāja Sutta (Snp 1.4 (PTS Snp 12))
**ID:** Snp 1.4 (PTS Snp 12)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Kasibhāradvāja Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp1.4
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kasibhāradvāja Sutta* (Snp 1.4) is a mixed prose-and-verse discourse set in the brahmin village (*brāhmaṇagāma*) of Ekanāḷā in Dakkhiṇāgiri, Magadha [Katre 1931; Saddhatissa 2013]. During the sowing season, while the brahmin farmer Kasībhāradvāja is working five hundred ploughs and distributing food to his laborers, the Buddha arrives seeking alms [Saddhatissa 2013]. Kasībhāradvāja rebukes the Buddha, arguing that recluses do not engage in productive labor and therefore do not deserve to eat [SuttaCentral; Winternitz 1933; IBC 2011; Okumura 2012]. The Buddha answers through an extended agricultural metaphor, explaining that he too ploughs and sows: faith is his seed, austerity (*tapas*) is the rain, wisdom is his yoke and plough [Norman 1997-2001; Hazra 1994], and his effort is a yoked ox that draws him without turning back (*anivattanta*) to nirvāṇa [Gilks]. The offering of milk-rice subsequently sizzles and smokes when discarded into water, likened to a heated ploughshare quenched in water [IBC 2011].
Text-critical analysis notes that the verses are divided by intervening prose that bridges the narrative, with a comparison against the parallel in the *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 7.11) suggesting that the *Suttanipāta* preserves an expanded prose redaction [Katre 1931]. In the verse summaries (*uddāna*) of the collection, its name is abbreviated simply as *Kasi* [Norman 1997-2001]. The sutta is also included in extended recensions of the protective chant anthology, the *Catubhāṇavārapāḷi* [Anālayo 2018].
Curated parallels recorded by SuttaCentral include SN 7.11, Snp 3.4 (*Pūraḷāsa*), SN 7.8, and SN 7.9, along with references in Mil 5.5.9, Sanskrit fragments (SF 25), and several Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* parallels (SĀ 98, SĀ2 264, SĀ3 1) [SuttaCentral; Beal 1882]. DharmaNexus reinforces these correspondences, showing near-identical Pali reuse with the *Brāhmaṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 7, §0.1–12.4 sharing over 13,000 characters) and high cross-language alignment scores with Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* texts (T99, T100, T101) as well as the Sanskrit *Śayanāsanavastu* [DharmaNexus].
